message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"dfcd5d713eb37ed7f574e041e6c81d7b2b1af04dfec9342c21da6c949d881e96","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-or-class-c:lineage:51","source_registry_sha256":"ce8335c1d96ff7ed209bf236ba9a56fe92dfebd915bc0e2fa7fb830ee03f0f09","units":[{"unit_id":"sec03-u01","module_id":"sec03-m01","objective_ids":["sec03-u01"],"title":{"text":"Keeping right and yielding","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Keeping right is the default lane position, and leaving it puts the duty to yield on you.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03"]},{"text":"Lines across your lane tell you whether to stop or only yield, and the two are easy to mix up.","fact_ids":["sec03-F36","sec03-R13"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Tara needs to go left of center to get around a stalled delivery van on a two-way road.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Going around an obstruction is an allowed reason to leave the right side, but being left of center means oncoming traffic has priority.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},"result":{"text":"Tara slows or stops until the oncoming traffic has gone by, then goes around the van.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a slow driver may drift toward the center line whenever it feels safer.","fact_ids":["sec03-F19","sec03-R06"]},"correction":{"text":"A slow driver keeps to the right lane or right edge and leaves it only to prepare for a left turn.","fact_ids":["sec03-R06","sec03-F19"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stay right, yield when left, stop at the bar.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F36"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You swing left of the center line to pass a parked garbage truck, and a car is coming toward you. Who has to give way?","fact_ids":["sec03-F03"]},"answer":{"text":"You do. Any time you are left of center, you yield to oncoming traffic.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03"]},"rationale":{"text":"Being left of center for any reason puts the duty to yield on you, and yielding means slowing or stopping so the other car continues safely.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Where you belong on the road","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Keep right is the default.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F04"]},{"text":"Yielding has a precise meaning.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F04"]},{"text":"Pavement lines tell you where to stop.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about where your car belongs on the road and who goes first when space is shared. Oregon's default is simple: keep to the right, with a short list of exceptions. Then there is the word yield, which shows up in many rules and has a precise meaning. To yield, you slow down or stop so that another driver or a pedestrian can carry on safely. Finally, the pavement itself carries instructions, with lines that tell you exactly where to stop and where to yield. By the end, you should be able to look at a lane situation and know whether you belong there and who has priority.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Keep right and its exceptions","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Passing a vehicle going your way.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},{"text":"Going around an obstruction.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},{"text":"One-way roads and a three-lane center passing lane.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},{"text":"When traffic personnel direct you.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"The keep-right rule is the starting point for every lane question. You stay on the right side of the road unless one of a few situations applies. You may move left when you are passing a vehicle traveling in your direction, or when something blocks your lane and you must go left of center to get around it. On a one-way road the rule does not hold you to the right, and on a three-lane road you may use its center passing lane. Finally, when traffic personnel tell you where to drive, you follow them. If a question describes leaving the right side for some other reason, be suspicious of that answer.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Sharing a road with no line","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"No center line: leave at least half.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},{"text":"Left of center: you yield.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},{"text":"Yield means slow or stop for others.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Some narrow two-way roads have no center line at all. That does not make the road a free-for-all. Each driver must leave at least half of the road for traffic coming the other way, so you share it rather than claiming the middle. On roads that do have a center line, a related rule applies. Whenever you are left of that line, whatever your reason, the duty to yield is yours, and oncoming traffic goes first. Remember what yielding means: you slow down or stop so the other vehicle or pedestrian can keep going safely. It does not always require a full stop, but it always puts the other road user first.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Driveways, alleys and lane changes","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"No signs or signals: stop before the road.","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Yield to vehicles and pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Change lanes only when safe, and rarely.","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Leaving private ground to join a road is a common trap. When you come out of an alley, a driveway or a parking lot and there are no signs or signals, you stop before you reach the road. Then you yield to the vehicles and pedestrians that are approaching. Notice that pedestrians are included, so a person walking past the driveway has priority too. Once you are on the road, lane changes follow a simple standard. Change lanes only when it is safe to do so, and avoid changing lanes frequently. A driver who weaves from lane to lane is not following that guidance, even if every single move looked clear.","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Slow drivers keep right","fact_ids":["sec03-F19","sec03-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Use the right lane or right edge.","fact_ids":["sec03-F19","sec03-R06"]},{"text":"Exception: preparing for a left turn.","fact_ids":["sec03-F19","sec03-R06"]},{"text":"Pull off to let a line pass.","fact_ids":["sec03-F19","sec03-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you are driving more slowly than the normal flow of traffic, the keep-right idea matters even more. Use the right lane, or stay close to the right edge of the road. The one exception is when you are getting ready to turn left, because then you need to position yourself for that turn. If a line of vehicles has built up behind you, do not simply carry on as if nothing has changed. Pull off at the first place where it is safe and let that line of traffic go by. The rule asks a slow driver to do two things: keep right, and clear the way at the first safe chance.","fact_ids":["sec03-F19","sec03-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Stop line or yield line","fact_ids":["sec03-F35","sec03-F36","sec03-R13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop line: solid white bar across your lane.","fact_ids":["sec03-F35","sec03-F36","sec03-R13"]},{"text":"Yield line: row of triangles pointing at you.","fact_ids":["sec03-F35","sec03-F36","sec03-R13"]},{"text":"Pedestrian in a crosswalk: you stop.","fact_ids":["sec03-F35","sec03-F36","sec03-R13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap that catches people who skim. Two pavement markings run across your lane, and they ask for different things. A stop line is a solid white line across your lane, and it marks the place where you must stop. A yield line is a row of triangles pointing toward you, and it marks where you must yield instead. Do not treat them as the same instruction. Nearby you may also find a marked crosswalk, drawn with white lines. When a pedestrian is in that crosswalk, you must stop. So always ask two questions: what does the marking require, and is someone already in front of you?","fact_ids":["sec03-F35","sec03-F36","sec03-R13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check: left of center","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"You go left of center around a parked truck.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},{"text":"A car approaches from ahead.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},{"text":"Who gives way?","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: picture yourself on a two-way road, swinging left of the center line to get past a parked garbage truck, when a car appears coming toward you. Who has to give way? The answer is you. Going around an obstruction is a valid reason to be left of center, but it does not hand you priority. Whenever you are on the left side of the center line, for any reason, you must yield to oncoming traffic. In practice that means slowing or stopping so the oncoming car can continue safely, and only then finishing your move around the truck. If you picked the other driver, revisit the yield rule.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Lane position in brief","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R06","sec03-F36","sec03-F35"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stay right unless an exception applies.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R06","sec03-F36","sec03-F35"]},{"text":"Left of center means you yield.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R06","sec03-F36","sec03-F35"]},{"text":"Bar means stop; triangles mean yield.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R06","sec03-F36","sec03-F35"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, keeping right is your default, and only a short list of situations lets you move left: passing, going around an obstruction, a one-way road, a three-lane road's center passing lane, or directions from traffic personnel. Whenever you are left of center, you yield, and yielding means slowing or stopping so others continue safely. Leaving a driveway, alley or parking lot with no signs or signals, stop and then yield to vehicles and pedestrians. Slow drivers keep right unless preparing to turn left. On the pavement, a solid bar means stop, triangles mean yield, and a pedestrian in a crosswalk means stop.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05","sec03-R06","sec03-F36","sec03-F35"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec03-u02","module_id":"sec03-m02","objective_ids":["sec03-u02"],"title":{"text":"Oregon These are called statutory limits, and the key idea is that they hold whether or not a sign is posted. If you turn into an alley or drive through a park, the limit is already there, even with no sign in sight. Only a posted sign showing another speed changes it. That is why knowing the figure for each type of place matters so much. We will climb the ladder from the slowest streets to the open road, and then look at the pairs that people most often confuse.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"How maximum limits work","fact_ids":["sec03-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"They apply on top of the basic rule.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07"]},{"text":"They mark the top safe speed in ideal conditions.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07"]},{"text":"A posted sign can set another speed.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Before the numbers, understand what a maximum limit is. Oregon's maximum limits apply on top of the basic rule, which means you must satisfy both at once. A maximum limit marks the top safe speed when conditions are ideal, so on a clear, dry, empty road it is the ceiling, not a target. Once conditions get worse, the basic rule may ask for less. The maximum limits hold whether or not they are posted, unless a sign shows a different speed. So a missing sign never means there is no limit. It means the statutory figure for that kind of place is the one you follow.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The low end of the ladder","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Alleys and narrow residential areas: fifteen.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},{"text":"Business districts and school zones: twenty.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},{"text":"Residential districts, parks, ocean shores: twenty-five.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the bottom of the ladder, in miles per hour. Alleys and narrow residential areas carry fifteen, the lowest statutory limit. Next comes twenty, which covers any business district and any school speed zone. Then twenty-five, which applies in residential districts, in public parks, and on ocean shores where vehicles are allowed. Picture the setting and ask how tight and busy it is. The tightest spaces, alleys and narrow residential streets, get the lowest figure. Shopping areas and school zones share the next step. Ordinary neighborhoods, parks and beaches open to vehicles sit one step higher.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Open roads and interstates","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Roads fitting no other category: fifty-five.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R03"]},{"text":"A posted sign can change it.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R03"]},{"text":"Interstate limits vary.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Above the town streets sits a catch-all figure. Any road that fits none of the other categories carries fifty-five miles per hour, unless a sign posts a different speed. Think of it as the default for roads left over after alleys, business districts, school zones, residential districts, parks and ocean shores are sorted out. Interstate highways are handled differently. Their limits vary rather than following one fixed statutory figure, so you watch the posted signs. On a practice question, if a road has no other category and no sign, choose fifty-five, and if it is an interstate, remember the limit is not one single number.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Narrow streets and school zones","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Narrow residential is lower than residential.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},{"text":"School zones match business districts.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},{"text":"Neither matches twenty-five.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two pairs cause most of the errors in this topic. First, narrow residential areas and residential districts sound like the same thing, but they are not. Alleys and narrow residential areas carry fifteen miles per hour, while ordinary residential districts carry twenty-five, so the narrowness of the street changes the limit. Second, school speed zones are easy to lump in with homes and parks, because schools sit in neighborhoods. Yet a school speed zone shares its limit of twenty with business districts, not the twenty-five used in residential districts and parks. When a question mentions either place, slow down and check which step it sits on.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-F09","sec03-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check: narrow lane","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R01","sec03-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"You leave a shopping street.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R01","sec03-F09"]},{"text":"You enter a narrow residential lane.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R01","sec03-F09"]},{"text":"No speed is posted.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R01","sec03-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you turn off a busy shopping street into a narrow residential lane, and no speed is posted anywhere. What is the statutory limit on that lane? The answer is fifteen miles per hour. Alleys and narrow residential areas carry the lowest statutory figure. Notice that the shopping street you just left was a business district, which carries twenty, so you are actually stepping down. If you answered twenty-five, you treated the lane as an ordinary residential district, which is the most common slip here. The narrowness of the street is what drops the limit to the bottom of the ladder.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08","sec03-R01","sec03-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"The speed ladder in brief","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, fifty-five.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R03"]},{"text":"Interstates vary.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R03"]},{"text":"No sign still means a limit.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"To pull it together, Oregon's statutory limits hold whether or not a sign is posted, and they apply on top of the basic rule. In miles per hour, alleys and narrow residential areas carry fifteen. Business districts and school speed zones carry twenty. Residential districts, public parks and ocean shores open to vehicles carry twenty-five. Roads that fit no other category carry fifty-five unless posted otherwise, and interstate limits vary. Watch the two classic mix-ups: a narrow residential street is lower than an ordinary residential district, and a school zone matches business districts rather than homes and parks.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-R01","sec03-R02","sec03-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec03-u03","module_id":"sec03-m03","objective_ids":["sec03-u03"],"title":{"text":"Basic rule and variable signs","fact_ids":["sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-F14"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The basic rule applies on every road at all times, so it can make a speed under the limit illegal.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Two kinds of variable speed signs look alike but carry very different legal weight.","fact_ids":["sec03-F13","sec03-F14","sec03-R04"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Ana sees a lit yellow sign recommending a lower speed as fog rolls over the highway, and she is still under the posted limit.","fact_ids":["sec03-F13","sec03-F15"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The yellow sign is advice rather than a limit, but police may enforce it through the basic rule, which asks what is reasonable and cautious in fog.","fact_ids":["sec03-F13","sec03-F16"]},"result":{"text":"Ana slows toward the recommended speed, because holding the posted limit in thick fog could break the basic rule.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-F15"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking any speed below the posted limit is automatically legal.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18"]},"correction":{"text":"A speed that is unsafe for conditions breaks the basic rule even when it is under the posted limit.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-R05"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Limit is the ceiling, conditions set the speed.","fact_ids":["sec03-R05","sec03-F16"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A black-and-white variable sign drops to a lower number as snow begins. Is the new number advice or a limit?","fact_ids":["sec03-F14"]},"answer":{"text":"It is a limit, enforced like any speed limit sign.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14"]},"rationale":{"text":"Black-and-white variable signs change the actual limit with conditions, while only the yellow variable signs are advisory.","fact_ids":["sec03-F14","sec03-R04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Choosing a lawful speed","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"The limit is a ceiling.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-R05"]},{"text":"Conditions decide your speed.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-R05"]},{"text":"Some signs change with the weather.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Knowing the speed limit is only half of choosing a lawful speed. In this lesson you will meet the basic rule, which asks whether your speed suits the conditions right now. You will see why a speed under the posted limit can still break the law, and why the limit itself is a ceiling you never go above. Then we turn to Oregon's variable speed signs, which change their numbers as conditions change. Some of them set the limit and some only give advice, and telling them apart is a common source of confusion. We finish with racing and with how speed affects a pedestrian who is struck.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The basic rule","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Reasonable and cautious for conditions.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-F17"]},{"text":"Every road, all the time.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-F17"]},{"text":"Weigh traffic, people, road and weather.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"The basic rule is short but powerful. It requires you to drive at a speed that is reasonable and cautious for the conditions that exist, on every road and at all times. There is no road where it switches off. To follow it, you weigh what is around you: other traffic, pedestrians and cyclists, the surface and width of the road, hazards at intersections, the weather, and how far you can see. Each of those can call for a slower speed. One thing the basic rule never does is permit you to go faster than the limit. It can only ask for less, never more.","fact_ids":["sec03-F16","sec03-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Under the limit, still illegal","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Unsafe for conditions breaks the rule.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-R05"]},{"text":"Being under the limit is no defense.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-R05"]},{"text":"Neither rule allows exceeding the limit.","fact_ids":["sec03-F18","sec03-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the idea that surprises many new drivers. A speed that is unsafe for the conditions breaks the basic rule even when it is below the posted limit. Imagine dense fog or a road slick with rain.
